Evaluating the Statistical Fidelity and Utility of Aggregated Patient Count as a Surrogate for

Line-Level EHR in Kidney-Transplant Analyses

## Abstract

Electronic Health Records (EHR) contain valuable information for clinical and population-level

studies, but the sharing of raw data is strictly constrained by privacy regulations. Cumulus

addresses this challenge by generating privacy-preserving aggregated patient-count data, termed

“CUBE”, which is a power set matrix of variable combinations with k-anonymity constraints.

However, the statistical fidelity and utility of CUBE data compared to traditional line-level EHR

remains unquantified. We conducted evaluations comparing CUBE and line-level EHR using

data from a cohort of patients with kidney transplant at the Boston Children’s Hospital. Our

approach includes: (1) implement Bayesian inference to model hidden information in the CUBE,

(2) evaluate the statistical fidelity between the original data and the CUBE, and (3) evaluate the

utility of CUBE in kidney-transplant-related analyses relative to using the original data. The

count inference pipeline outperformed baseline imputation strategies in recovering suppressed

counts, achieving mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.12 in a high-dimensional, low-cardinality

CUBE (10 variables, 57.1% of suppressed cells deterministically recovered) and MAE of 1.53 in

a lower-dimensional, high-cardinality CUBE (3 variables). Our results from the fidelity

evaluation demonstrated that the CUBE preserved marginal and joint distributions with

consistently low Jensen-Shannon divergence and retains pairwise associations with low mean

absolute difference of Cramér’s V against the original data. The results from the utility

evaluation demonstrated that the CUBE reproduced conclusions consistent with the original data


<!-- Page 4 -->


iii

in descriptive statistics, odds ratios, and classification performance. These findings show that

CUBE data retains sufficient statistical fidelity and utility for clinical research applications.

## Chapter 1: Introduction

ChatGPT 5.4 and Grammarly were used to proofread and refine for clarity and readability.

### 1.1: Background

Electronic Health Records (EHR) were widely adopted in the United States after the

HITECH Act (“National Trends in Hospital and Physician Adoption of Electronic Health

Records,” n.d.) and provided massive amounts of valuable information for clinical and

population-level studies (Casey et al., 2016). The development of the SMART/HL7 FHIR Bulk

Data Access API further enabled the extraction of standardized patient-level data at scale across

populations, yet the sharing of raw data remains constrained by HIPAA privacy regulations

(Mandl et al., 2020). Due to the sensitivity of health information, data access approval processes

can be lengthy while the analytical value of the data cannot be assessed prior to access.

To address these challenges of exchanging EHR data at scale, Cumulus was proposed.

Cumulus is a system that generates population-level aggregated patient counts (“CUBE” data) of

selected variables across federated healthcare organizations (HCOs). Within each HCO, patient-

level data are extracted with FHIR APIs, preprocessed with ETL and AI/NLP pipelines, and

converted to an aggregated matrix, a power set of all variable combinations, with k-anonymity

constraints where counts less than k (10 for Cumulus) are removed. Aggregated matrices from

multiple HCOs can also be summed and accessed through the Cumulus dashboard. The CUBE

data preserves individual privacy and can be near-instantaneously accessed by authorized users

(McMurry et al., 2024).


<!-- Page 11 -->


2

Recently, unpublished work from researchers collaborating with the Mandl lab had

demonstrated the potential of using CUBE data for cluster analyses by replicating a clustering

analysis related to diabetes. However, a quantifiable evaluation framework to assess the

statistical information retention and loss of CUBE data compared to line-level data has yet to be

established. This project aims to evaluate the statistical fidelity and utility of CUBE data on

patients with kidney transplant surgeries in the Boston Children’s Hospital.

Kidney transplantation has been a life-saving procedure that allows patients with severe

organ failure to receive a healthy kidney. However, there are still risks of graft rejection, an

immune response against the foreign organ after transplantation (Elalouf, 2023).

Immunosuppressive drugs are often prescribed to suppress immune responses against the

transplanted organs but can consequently increase the risk of infections (Elalouf, 2023; Fishman,

n.d.). Furthermore, individual responses to immunosuppressive treatments can vary, which makes

it hard to generalize treatments (Drabe et al., 2019). Therefore, it’s important to monitor

individuals consistently and maintain the balance between considerations for graft rejection and

infection. Traditional line-level EHR data, with each patient as a row entry, have demonstrated

utility in analyzing outpatient organ transplant outcomes (Cohen et al., 2020). Now, we aim to

evaluate whether the CUBE-formatted data retains statistical fidelity that allows comparable

utility in kidney-transplant data analysis.

The goal of this project is to establish an evaluation framework for understanding how

privacy-preserving aggregation and thresholding of patient-level data into population-level data

influence the statistical fidelity and utility of EHR data. Specifically, this project aims to (1) infer

the counts suppressed by k-anonymity in the CUBE to recover a more complete representation of

the data for downstream evaluation, (2) evaluate the statistical fidelity between the original data


<!-- Page 12 -->


3

and the CUBE, and (3) evaluate the utility of CUBE in kidney-transplant-related analyses

relative to using the original data.

### 1.2: Data

The dataset used in this study was compiled from a cohort of kidney transplant patients at

Boston Children’s Hospital. Patients were identified using inclusion criteria with study period

after 2021, at least one kidney transplant-related diagnosis or procedure code, and at least two

clinical encounters. The final cohort included 285 patients with kidney transplant. For each

selected patient, the dataset contained the full available longitudinal history (not restricted to the

post-transplant period) of key clinical study variables, including demographics, conditions, and

medications.

### 1.3: CTGAN Synthetic Data Generation as a Baseline Comparison

Another well-studied privacy-preserving data sharing strategy is the generation of

synthetic data based on the original data (Beaulieu-Jones et al., 2019). Generative models are

trained on the original data to learn its statistical structure and produce synthetic patient samples

that preserve patterns of the original data. To provide a comparative baseline for the fidelity and

utility evaluations on the CUBE, synthetic sets of patient records of the same size as the original

data were generated using the Conditional Tabular GAN (CTGAN) method (Xu et al., 2019).

The same fidelity and utility evaluation applied to the CUBE data were applied to the synthetic

data against the original. This comparison contextualizes the information retention of the CUBE

relative to another privacy-preserving data sharing method in terms of the statistical fidelity and

downstream analytical utility in kidney transplant research.

## Chapter 2: Aim 1 – Infer hidden information in the CUBE

ChatGPT 5.4 and Grammarly were used to proofread and refine for clarity and readability.

The CUBE applies k-anonymity suppression to protect patient privacy such that any

aggregate count fewer than the suppression threshold k is suppressed from the published data

(represented as NA). In the Cumulus system, the threshold is set to k = 10 patients, which means

counts fewer than 10 are suppressed. Counts for every possible combination of grouping

variables (e.g., total number of patients, all single-variable marginals, all two-variable marginals,

etc.) that are above 10 are published. These overlapping aggregates create a system of equations

that may reveal information about the hidden counts. They may narrow the range of possible

values for a suppressed cell, and in the extreme case, may deterministically recover a suppressed

count. To evaluate the fidelity and utility of the CUBE with a more accurate information content,

this aim develops a count inference pipeline that produces a posterior probability distribution of

each suppressed count based on the published portion of the CUBE.


<!-- Page 14 -->


5

### 2.1: Methods

The CUBE data format can be understood as the output of a Trino CUBE operation,

which produce aggregate counts for every element of the powerset of grouping variables, and the

suppression rule replaces any count below the threshold k with null values. Given a dataset of N

individual patient records, each described by v categorical variables, the CUBE operation

produces aggregate counts for every possible subset of grouping variables. Grouping by zero

variables gives the grand total N representing the number of patients. Grouping by one variable

produces v sets of single-variable marginals. Grouping by pairs of variables produces sets of two-

variable cross tabulations. And grouping by all v variables produces sets of unique combination

of all variable levels which are the atomic-level cells that can be directly converted back to

individual records. Each aggregate count in the CUBE can also be viewed as a sum over a set of

atomic cells. For example, the marginal count for “Male” equals the sum of all atomic cells

where the gender variable is “Male”.

Published aggregate counts establish equations where the sum of counts of its constituent

atomic cells equals to the published count. Suppressed aggregates establish inequalities where

the counts are between zero and the suppression threshold k. From the published system of

equations, the tightest possible range for each atomic cell count that are mathematically

consistent with the system can be calculated by two integer linear programs (ILPs) (Abowd et

al., 2025). For each cell, the first obtains the lower bound by finding the minimum count that

satisfies the system, and the second obtains the upper bound by finding the maximum count that

satisfies the system (Dobra & Fienberg, 2000). In the case that the lower bound equals the upper

bound, the suppressed count can be deterministically recovered by the published counts since


<!-- Page 15 -->


6

there only exists one integer value consistent with all constraints. In other cases, the lower and

upper bounds define the possible range of counts for the cell.

The deterministic bounds describe the set of values that are mathematically possible for

each suppressed count but do not distinguish which values are more probable within the range. A

Bayesian model was used to obtain a probability distribution over the suppressed counts with the

published data (Diaconis & Sturmfels, 1998). Each atomic cell j was modeled as an independent

draw from a Poisson distribution with rate parameter 𝜆𝑗, representing the expected count for each

cell and has a log-normal prior:

Posterior samples were drawn using the No-U-Turn Sampler (Hoffman & Gelman, 2011),

each consists of a set of atomic cell rates. Metropolis-Hasting sampling (Robert, 2016) was used

to generate integer count vectors for each posterior samples that fully satisfies all published

equalities and derived bounds and are probable given the rates of the posterior sample. Each of

the resulting samples, representing a plausible combination of counts for the atomic cells, were

aggregated to get the marginal counts for every variable combination within the sample to be in

the same format as the CUBE. These completed CUBE samples were then used in the fidelity

and utility evaluations described in Aims 2 and 3.

### 2.2: Results

The count inference pipeline was applied to two examples of CUBE generated with study

variables related to kidney transplant research.

2.2.1: Example 1 – Race x Gender x Age

In the first example, the CUBE was constructed from three demographic variables within

the kidney transplant patient cohort: race, gender, and age. The CUBE produced 264 total cells,

each representing a variable value combination, where 50 (18.9%) had counts above the

suppression threshold k=10 and were published directly. Among the remaining suppressed cells,

12 (4.5%) were deterministically recovered such that only one integer value was consistent with

all the published equations, and 202 (76.5%) remained uncertain. Figure 1 shows a few of the

count inference output for the Race x Gender x Age CUBE. Each row corresponds to one cell

from the CUBE with the ILP-derived bounds, the posterior mean and standard deviation of the

inferred counts and the actual count from the original data. The cells that can be deterministically

recovered shows lower bound equal to upper bound in the bound column, and the cells that

remained uncertain have bounds at most between 0 to 9, with some being narrower like the

group with [gender=female, race=other race, age=16] having a bound between 0 and 6.

The inferred counts from the pipeline were also compared against the true counts from

the original data to examine how well the pipeline estimated the counts. Mean absolute error

(MAE) was calculated between the inferred counts and the true counts for each posterior CUBE

samples. The mean across the samples and the 95% credible interval was reported. The MAE

from using several baseline strategies were also calculated for comparison. Table 2 shows the

MAE comparisons for the atomic cells. The CUBE count inference posterior mean achieved the

lowest MAE of 1.5291 across all cells compared to 1.5765 when the suppressed counts were

assumed to be zero, 3.7059 when the suppressed counts were assumed to be five (midpoint),

3.9118 when suppressed counts were randomly imputed between 0 and 9, and 1.6765 for the

CTGAN-generated data. On average, the inferred counts were around 1.5291 patients away from

the actual count with a 95% credible interval between 1.1698 and 1.9245.

In the high-dimension, low-cardinality example (Race x Gender x 7 Medication Class x

Graft Rejection CUBE), the count inference pipeline achieved strong recovery, substantially

outperforming all baselines. In the low-dimension, high-cardinality example (Race x Gender x

Age CUBE), the pipeline achieved the lowest MAE but showed only marginal improvement over

the zero-imputation and CTGAN data generation method. It should also be noted that there can

be cases where large portion of suppressed counts could be deterministically recovered using

integer linear programming. The sharing of the CUBE will still be limited to restricted groups

instead of to the public, so privacy considerations are not the major evaluation in this project.

Nevertheless, running the count inference pipeline can still serve as a minimal privacy evaluation

before sharing to understand the extent of small subgroups of patients that can be

deterministically recovered.

## Chapter 3: Aim 2 – Evaluate the statistical fidelity of CUBE

ChatGPT 5.4 and Grammarly were used to proofread and refine for clarity and readability.

The count inference pipeline produced many samples consistent with the published

counts of the CUBE. Each sample is like a CUBE without hidden information but with estimates

of the hidden information. These can then be reconstructed to line-level records by repeating

each atomic cell by its corresponding inferred counts. This aim evaluates the statistical fidelity of

the CUBE by comparing each of the inferred CUBE samples against the original line-level data

to see how closely the CUBE resembles the original data based on statistical measures.

### 3.1: Methods

Statistical fidelity was evaluated along three complementary dimensions: distribution,

association (Adams et al., 2024) and variance. Each fidelity metric was computed per sample and

summarized across samples to provide point estimates and uncertainty. The same fidelity metrics

were computed using the CTGAN-generated data against the original data to provide a

comparison.

The Jensen-Shannon divergence (JSD) was used to quantify the similarity of probability

distributions (Lin, 1991) between the original data and the CUBE. JSD between each of the

CUBE sample and the original data were calculated for each marginal distribution and the full

joint distribution.

The Cramér’s V was used to assess the strength of pairwise associations between

variables. For each pair of variables, Cramér’s V was calculated from the original data and from


<!-- Page 24 -->


15

the CUBE samples, and the absolute difference between the Cramér’s V of the two data was used

to evaluate how well the CUBE preserves variable relationships.

Coefficient of Determination (R2) was used to provide a more intuitive summary of

fidelity at the atomic cell level. R2 was computed between the vector of atomic cell counts of the

original data and the vector of inferred atomic counts of each CUBE sample.


<!-- Page 25 -->


16

### 3.2: Results

The fidelity evaluation was applied to the same two CUBE examples from Aim 1.

3.2.1: Example 1 – Race x Gender x Age

For each of the inferred CUBE samples, JSD was computed against the original data,

each represents how far a plausible version of the CUBE differs from the original data. Figure 3

shows the mean JSD across inferred CUBE samples with error bars representing the 95%

credible interval and the JSD between the CTGAN-generated data and original data for each

marginal distribution and the full joint distribution. JSD is bounded between 0 and 1 with 0

meaning the two distributions are identical and larger JSD meaning the distributions are more

different. The mean JSD for gender, race and age using the CUBE samples are 0 (95% CI: [0,

0]), 0.0049 (95% CI: [0.0002, 0.0060]) and 0.0083 (95% CI: [0.0012, 0.0212]) respectively, and

the JSD for gender, race and age using the CTGAN-generated data is 0.0004, 0.0184 and 0.1266

respectively. The near-zero marginal JSD values for the CUBE indicate that the individual

variable distributions are nearly identical to the original data. The mean JSD for the joint

distribution using the CUBE is 0.1049 (95% CI: [0.0713, 0.1476]), and the JSD for the joint

distribution using the CTGAN-generated data is 0.3007. In comparison, the CUBE produced

consistently lower JSD values than the CTGAN-generated data across all marginal distributions

and the joint distribution, demonstrating better preservation of distribution fidelity of the original

data.

Cramér’s V was computed for every pair of variables in the original, inferred CUBE

samples, and the CTGAN-generated data. Table 5 shows the absolute difference of Cramer’s V

between the original and the CUBE samples for every variable pair as well as the absolute

difference of Cramer’s V between the original and the CTGAN-generated data for every variable

pair. For the CUBE samples, the absolute difference against the original data for gender x race is

0.0479, for gender x age is 0.0749, and for race x age is 0.1704. For the CTGAN-generated data,

the absolute difference against the original data for gender x race is 0.0662, for gender x age is

slightly lower absolute differences for the gender x age and race x age pairs indicating that the

CUBE samples were less effective in preserving variable associations than the CTGAN data

generation method. The larger absolute difference of Cramér’s V in the CUBE indicates that the

count inference uncertainty in this low-dimensional, high-cardinality CUBE introduced more

### 4.2: Odds Ratio

Beyond descriptive summaries, researchers are often interested in the risk of outcome for

certain demographic or clinical subgroup relative to others. To evaluate whether the CUBE

preserves results from risk analyses, odds ratio analysis was applied to the Race x Gender x 7

Medication Class x Graft Rejection CUBE to investigate the odds of graft rejection for patients

receiving each combination of drug class in each demographic compared to all other groups

combined. Each CUBE sample was used to calculate the odds ratio for every subgroup and

averaged to compare against the odds ratio calculated with the original data. The mean absolute

difference between the log odds ratio of the CUBE and the original data across all subgroups is

0.0084, and the mean absolute difference between the log odds ratio of the CTGAN-generated

data and original data is 5.5633. More importantly, when using the CTGAN-generated data to

calculate the odds ratio, 25 out of the 106 subgroups had a odds ratio that would give different

clinical interpretation than if the original data was used to calculate the odds ratio. Odds ratio

greater than 1 suggests higher odds of the outcome in the group while odds ratio below 1

suggests lower odds of the outcome in the group. When the direction of the odds ratio changed,

the clinical interpretation of the risk for the patient subgroup would be different. The CUBE did

not show any cases where the direction of the odds ratio changed relative to the original data

which further supports the CUBE’s utility in odds ratio analyses.

### 4.3: Predictive Modeling

Another area of analysis included in the utility evaluation is predictive modeling for

clinical outcomes. To evaluate whether the CUBE preserves classification performance, a logistic

regression classifier was trained on the Race x Gender x 7 Medication Class x Graft Rejection

CUBE to predict graft rejection from the rest of the features. The original data was split into 80%

for training and 20% was held out with stratification for evaluating the classification

performance. The training set of patients was converted into CUBE format, and the count

inference pipeline was applied to generate CUBE samples with count estimates. Each of the

sample were used to train the classifier and evaluated on the held-out test set from the original

data. The accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 scores were averaged across the samples with 95%

credible interval reported. CTGAN-generated data was also used as a comparative baseline. The

training set from the original data was used to generate the CTGAN-generated data and the

CTGAN-generated data was used to train the classifier. The held-out test set was used to evaluate

the classification performance of the model trained with the CTGAN-generated data. Table 8

shows the accuracy, precision, recall, and f1obtained from models trained with the original data,

CUBE samples, and the CTGAN-generated data. All the classification performances were very

weak, but the performance metrics of the CUBE data is comparable to the original data while the

performance of model trained with the CTGAN-generated data were much more different than

the original data. Because all models performed near-chance, this comparison confirms that the

CUBE does not introduce spurious signal rather than demonstrating predictive utility.

## Chapter 5: Discussion

ChatGPT 5.4 and Grammarly were used to proofread and refine for clarity and readability.

### 5.1: Interpretations

This project established an evaluation framework for understanding the statistical

information content of privacy-preserving CUBE data on a cohort of 285 kidney transplant

patients at Boston Children’s Hospital. Across the fidelity and utility evaluations, the results

consistently demonstrated that the CUBE retains substantial statistical information from the

original line-level data and provides comparable results and interpretation for analytical analyses.

The count inference pipeline developed in Aim 1 utilized the overlapping system of

equations released in the CUBE’s powerset structure to recover hidden information. In the Race

x Gender x Age example, only three variables are involved, but both the gender and age variable

contained many categories, leading to many subgroups with very few patients. 4.5% of the

suppressed cells were deterministically recovered, and the mean absolute error on the count

estimates was 1.5291 which means on average the inferred count is around 1.5291 from the

actual count. The other baselines had a MAE of 1.5767 for zero-imputation, 3.7059 for midpoint-

imputation, 3.9118 for random-imputation and 1.6765 for using CTGAN-generated data which

are all above the MAE of the count inference method. Although the count inference pipeline

MAE were the lowest for this, it was only slightly lower than the zero-imputation and CTGAN

data generation method. This is likely because the age variable contained many categories (each

age is a category) which produced many atomic cells with very few patients. The CUBE and

count inference pipeline are weaker in these high-cardinality settings, but still slightly better than


<!-- Page 39 -->


30

the baselines compared here, because of high proportion of suppressed counts and fewer

published information to anchor the inference.

In the Race x Gender x 7 Medication Classes x Graft Rejection example, 10 variables are

involved and most of them are binary variables. 57.1% of the suppressed cells were

deterministically recovered, and the MAE was 0.1203 (well-below the other baseline MAEs).

This illustrates a fundamental property of the CUBE that as the number of variables increases

and the number of categories within variables decreases, more information appears in the

overlapping equations used for inference which narrows the room for uncertainty.

The findings from the two examples connect to a broader understanding of disclosure

risk. Simple suppression of small counts does not guarantee privacy given the structure of the

CUBE and the count inference pipeline demonstrated the possibilities of recovering single

patients. While the Cumulus system restricts CUBE access to authorized users rather than the

public, the privacy risks should be aware of for every release of the CUBE, potentially using the

ILP-based bound computation as a screening tool.

The fidelity evaluation in Aim 2 revealed that the CUBE preserves the distributional

properties of the original data with high accuracy across both examples. The JSD between CUBE

samples and the original data was consistently lower than that between the CTGAN-generated

data and the original. The CUBE publishes exact counts for cells above the suppression

threshold, and the count inference pipeline further narrows uncertainties for the suppressed cells

which inherently limits high distortion of the distribution patterns. In contrast, CTGAN learns

the entire data generating process, making it susceptible to noise and can often distort tail

distributions and rare category combinations (Snoke et al., 2017).


<!-- Page 40 -->


31

The pairwise association results from Cramér’s V analysis demonstrated that the

CTGAN-generated data may sometimes outperform CUBE in variable association preservation

in low-dimensional, high-category examples. The count inference on CUBE is generally more

uncertain when the joint distribution contains many groups with very few patients which may

distort the bivariate associations more. However, in the higher-dimensional example, the CUBE

outperformed the CTGAN-generated data much more.

The R2 results reinforced the dimensionality and cardinality effect where both the CUBE

and the CTGAN-generated data had a low R2 in the Race x Gender x Age example reflecting

uncertainty in atomic cell counts. In the Race x Gender x 7 Medication Classes x Graft Rejection

example, the CUBE’s R2 rose to 0.9854 while the CTGAN-generated data only had 0.5587. This

aligns with the results from the count inference pipeline where CUBE allows for dramatic drop

in uncertainty and large improvement in explained variance when the system contains more

informed equations.

The utility evaluation demonstrated that the CUBE’s statistical fidelity translates directly

into preserved analytical conclusions. Marginal probability estimates from the CUBE matched

the original data with very small mean absolute differences across all demographic variables.

The cumulative distribution function for age also showed visually comparable pattern between

the CUBE and original data, whereas that for the CTGAN-generated data shows a relatively

different pattern. These results affirm that basic descriptive analysis can be reliably performed

using the CUBE data.

The odds ratio analysis demonstrated that the CUBE maintained consistent odds ratio

directionality across all subgroups while the CTGAN-generated data produced 25 subgroups

with flipped odds ratio which would lead to opposite clinical interpretations about the risk of


<!-- Page 41 -->


32

graft rejection for the subgroup. This finding is critical in the context of kidney transplant as it

can lead to false risk assessments for the risk of graft rejection for patients in certain

demographic receiving certain combinations of medications. The magnitude of difference

between the log odds ratio of the CUBE and the original data is also much smaller than the

CTGAN-generated data comparing to the original data, indicating that the CUBE preserves both

the directionality and magnitudes of odds ratio better than CTGAN-generated data.

The classification results, while showing weak overall predictive performance with the

features selected in the example, CUBE was consistent with the performance of the original data.

The weak classification performance suggests that the available demographic and medication

class variables do not provide strong predictive signal for graft rejection. The model trained with

CUBE replicated this weak performance pattern, which would give researchers the same

conclusion as using the original data. The model trained with the CTGAN-generated data

showed poor performance, but the precision, recall, and f1 score dropped to zero which showed

that the model failed to predict any positive cases of graft rejection indicating distortion of the

feature and outcome relationships.

These fidelity and utility evaluation results together demonstrated that the CUBE retains

sufficient statistical properties and analytical utility for kidney transplant research. Compared to

CTGAN-generated data generation, the CUBE produces more similar properties and analytical

results to the original data.

### 5.2: Limitations and Future Direction

The evaluation was conducted on a single cohort of 285 kidney transplant patients from

Boston Children’s Hospital. The generalizability of these findings to larger cohorts, different

disease domains and different institutions remain to be investigated. The study also only

examined categorical variables. The CUBE discretized continuous variables in Cumulus for the

powerset aggregation which would introduce discretization loss that was not evaluated in this

study. The choice of the discretization strategy can also significantly influence the fidelity and

utility. A systematic evaluation on the discretization effect on the CUBE can be an interesting

direction in the future.

This study also only used one baseline, a synthetic data generation method, for

comparing evaluation results with. While CTGAN is widely used benchmark for tabular data

synthesis, a broader comparison with other synthetic data generation methods or privacy-

preserving data sharing methods like differential privacy would provide a more comprehensive

interpretation for the CUBE’s relative performance.

The utility evaluation focused only on a small set of downstream analyses related to

kidney transplant research. Other analytical tasks related to time-series analyses were excluded

from the current scope for the study but remains to be a potential next step for evaluating the

CUBE’s utility for complex analyses.

A formal privacy analysis was not conducted in the study, but a small experiment was

conducted to test the results of different k-thresholds (k=15, 30, 50) in replacement of the current

k=10 setting. There’s a clear trend that as the k increase, the number of deterministically

recoverable cells decreases and the MAE of the count inference increases. However, a large


<!-- Page 43 -->


34

number of cells can still be deterministically recovered, supporting the conclusion that simple k-

anonymity threshold alone may provide less privacy protection than intended. A future direction

can experiment how addition suppression and blurring strategies such as secondary suppression

algorithms and differential privacy, may affect the fidelity and utility.


<!-- Page 44 -->


35

### 5.3: Conclusion

This project developed an inference pipeline and evaluation framework to assess the

information content of the CUBE, a privacy-preserving aggregated data format produced by the

Cumulus system. The fidelity evaluation demonstrated that the CUBE retains substantial

statistical information showing the CUBE preserves distributions and pairwise associations of

the original data. The utility evaluation confirms that descriptive statistics, odds ratio, and

classification performance derived from the CUBE led to the same analytical conclusions as the

original data. At the same time, the analysis revealed that CUBEs with predominately binary

variables can be vulnerable to deterministic count recovery, so the privacy risks should still be

considered. The project also provided a reusable inference and evaluation framework that can be

used to evaluate the privacy, fidelity and utility of individual CUBE cases. Overall, these results

show that the CUBE can serve as an alternative to line-level data in kidney transplant research on

descriptive and analytical analyses with sufficient fidelity and utility.
